601.quote_or_event: “Wealth will not protect a careless man in this world and the next. Though he had seen the right way, he does not see it, even as one in the dark whose lamp has suddenly been put out.”
601.explanation: Mahavira's sermon on carelessness (pramāda) says that a negligent person loses even the light he once had, like a man whose lamp suddenly goes out in the dark.
601.tie_back: Valluvar's family-lamp that sloth dims and puts out has a close counterpart in the Jain image of the careless man whose lamp is put out.
601._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi's text on sacred-texts.com. The lamp image matches closely, but the Jain verse is about one person's spiritual sight, while the Kural is about a family's standing.

602.quote_or_event: “As the fallow leaf of the tree falls to the ground, when its days are gone, even so the life of men (will come to its close); Gautama, be careful all the while!”
602.explanation: Mahavira's famous refrain to Gautama (samayaṃ Goyama mā pamāyae, 'do not be careless even for a moment') makes constant vigilance against negligence the core discipline.
602.tie_back: Like the Kural's call to treat sloth as sloth and kill it in one's conduct, Mahavira tells his foremost disciple never to let carelessness in for a moment.
602._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Jain pramāda (carelessness) covers sloth but is wider and aimed at liberation, and the Kural's concern for the family is missing.

603.quote_or_event: “You cannot prolong your life, therefore be not careless; you are past help when old age approaches. Consider this: what (protection) will careless people get, who kill living beings and do not exert themselves?”
603.explanation: The fourth lecture warns that the careless, who will not exert themselves, have no protection when their end comes.
603.tie_back: The Kural's fool who clings to destructive sloth and perishes is the Jain 'careless' person who does not exert himself and finds no protection.
603._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. The theme of ruin through non-exertion is strong, but the Kural's point that the family dies before the man is absent, and the Jain verse adds harming living beings (ahimsa).

604.quote_or_event: “There are five causes which render wholesome discipline impossible: egoism, delusion, carelessness, illness, and idleness.”
604.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana counts carelessness and idleness among the causes that make right discipline impossible, so faults multiply where they take hold.
604.tie_back: Valluvar says that for those sunk in sloth faults keep multiplying; the Jain text names idleness as one of the roots that block all wholesome discipline.
604._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. It clearly names idleness as a source of failure, but it is a monastic list and does not speak of a family's decline.

605.quote_or_event: “'If he does not get (victory over his will) early, he will get it afterwards;' such reasoning presupposes the eternity of human life. But such a man despairs when his life draws to its close, and the dissolution of his body approaches.”
605.explanation: The text attacks procrastination: putting off effort assumes life lasts for ever. The same lecture (4.6) urges, 'Though others sleep, be thou awake!'
605.tie_back: Two of the Kural's four vices on the 'pleasure boat' to ruin, procrastination and oversleeping, are exactly what Uttaradhyayana 4 condemns.
605.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 4.9; cf. 4.6 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)
605._accuracy_note: Verse 4.9 checked word for word on sacred-texts.com, and 4.6 is paraphrased from the same page. Two of the Kural's four vices (procrastination, sleep) are covered; forgetfulness and the boat image are not.

606.quote_or_event: “Though one believe in the Law, he will rarely practise it; for people are engrossed by pleasures; Gautama, &c.”
606.explanation: In the 'Leaf of the Tree' sermon, Mahavira lists the rare advantages a soul may gain (human birth, hearing and believing the Law) and warns that even these are wasted by those who will not act on them.
606.tie_back: As the lazy heir gets no good from a world-ruler's wealth, the Jain soul handed rare spiritual fortune gains nothing if it will not exert itself.
606._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com, but this is only a next-best match: the parallel is wasted good fortune, while the Kural speaks literally of inherited royal wealth.

607.quote_or_event: “'As are bad pupils, so are bad bullocks; I shall leave these lazy donkeys, and shall practise severe austerities.'”
607.explanation: The sage Garga compares pupils who 'break down through want of zeal' to stubborn bullocks, then dismisses them in disgust as lazy donkeys.
607.tie_back: The Kural warns that the slothful will hear harsh rebuke and scorn; Garga's scornful words for his lazy pupils are exactly that kind of rebuke.
607.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 27.16; cf. 27.8 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)
607._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. This is a narrative example of the scorn the lazy earn, close to the Kural, though set among monks rather than in society at large.

608.quote_or_event: “Self is the one invincible foe, (together with the four) cardinal passions, (viz. anger, pride, deceit, and greed, they are five) and the (five) senses (make ten). These (foes), O great sage, I have regularly vanquished.”
608.explanation: Gautama tells Kesi that the real enemies are the unconquered self, the passions and the senses, and only someone who conquers them is free; the rest are held in their bondage.
608.tie_back: Valluvar warns that sloth turns the noble-born into slaves of their enemies; in Jainism, the person who does not exert himself stays bound to his inner enemies, the passions.
608._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Only a next-best match: it turns the Kural's political enemies into inner ones and does not mention sloth or noble birth.

609.quote_or_event: “By conquering his will, (a monk) reaches liberation, as a well-broken horse which is clad in harness (goes to battle). Be watchful in your young years; for thereby a monk quickly obtains liberation.”
609.explanation: The text holds that once the will is mastered and vigilance takes the place of negligence, faults fall away and freedom follows.
609.tie_back: As the Kural says faults vanish when a man throws off sloth's rule over him, the Jain sutra says conquering one's own will, like breaking in a horse, removes what holds a person back.
609._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. The remedy matches (self-mastery and vigilance end the fault), but the Jain goal is liberation, not restoring family and manly worth.

610.quote_or_event: Jain narrative tradition has its own version of the three strides. When the minister Namuci, ruling for a few days, threatened to kill the Jain monks, the ascetic Viṣṇukumāra, brother of King Mahāpadma, came in the form of a dwarf, asked for three paces of ground, and by his ascetic powers grew vast enough to cover the world and defeat Namuci.
610.explanation: In Jain tellings the three strides belong not to a god but to a monk whose powers came from tireless austerity and who used them to protect the community.
610.tie_back: The Kural's unsluggish king who gains all that the strider measured has a Jain parallel in the three strides themselves, credited to ascetic striving rather than to Vishnu.
610.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra VI.8 (Mahāpadmacakricaritra), vv. 148-203 (tr. Helen M. Johnson, vol. IV, pp. 99-102); also Vividhatīrthakalpa (Hastināpura-kalpa)
610._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. The story's existence and its location (Triṣaṣṭi VI.8, Johnson IV pp. 99-102) were confirmed through wisdomlib.org's index and glossary, but I did not read Johnson's full text; the parallel is to the Kural's Vamana allusion, not its point about a king's effort, and Jainism rejects Vishnu as a world-striding god.
